hook.text: Airbnb charges guests a service fee and hosts a commission. Both sides pay for the connection.

buildup.text: Marketplace commissions typically range from 10-30%. The platform adds value by matching supply to demand.

discovery.text: Uber takes 25% of every ride. The driver does the work; Uber provides the match and the payment.

twist.text: Once a marketplace dominates, sellers can't leave. Amazon sellers accept 15% fees because that's where buyers are.

climax.text: Two-sided marketplace fees are powerful because leaving means losing access to the other side.

punchline.text: Connect buyers and sellers, then tax every transaction. Simple power.

quiz.question: Why can dominant marketplaces charge high commissions?

details.summary: Marketplace commissions are percentage-based fees that platforms charge on each transaction completed between buyers and sellers. eBay charges sellers up to 15%, Airbnb takes 3% from hosts and up to 14% from guests, and food delivery apps take 15-30% from restaurants.
details.whyItMatters: Commission revenue directly ties platform income to transaction volume. The commission rate must be set low enough to attract participants but high enough to fund platform operations and generate profit, making it a critical strategic lever.
takeaways: Platforms take a percentage of every transaction between participants
Rates vary from 3% to 30% depending on the value platforms add
Commissions must balance revenue needs against participant retention

faq.question: What factors determine how high a marketplace commission can be?
faq.answer: The value the platform adds through demand generation, trust, payment processing, and logistics. The availability of alternatives for participants. The transaction size, as higher percentage fees are tolerable on smaller transactions. Industry norms and competitive pressure also constrain rates.

faq.question: How do marketplaces evolve their commission structures over time?
faq.answer: Many start with low or zero commissions to attract participants, then gradually increase rates as network effects strengthen. Others introduce tiered commissions, advertising fees, and premium placement charges that add revenue without raising the base transaction commission.
